record.original_question: Extend Chaitin complexity from finite strings to infinite strings, either by using non-terminating programs that run forever and generate infinite strings over infinite time, or by using computational models that process infinite strings in finite time, such as cellular automata or functions on reals.

evidence.quote: Chaitin complexity has been defined for finite strings. It would be interesting to extend it to infinite strings. Two ways can be envisaged: (a) using non-terminating programs, looping forever, and generating infinite strings in an infinite amount of time; (b) using computational models dealing with infinite strings in finite amounts of time (cellular automata, functions on reals, etc.).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $U$ be a universal prefix-free Turing machine. The Chaitin (prefix-free Kolmogorov) complexity of a finite binary string $x \in \{0,1\}^*$ is
$$H(x) \;=\; \min\{|p| : p \in \{0,1\}^*,\ U(p)=x\},$$
where $|p|$ denotes the length of the program $p$. This quantity is defined only for finite strings, since $U$ is required to halt and output a finite string.

Problem. Develop a meaningful extension of Chaitin complexity to infinite binary strings $\xi \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$. Specifically, give a rigorous definition of a complexity functional
$$H^\infty : \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \longrightarrow [0,\infty]$$
together with the proofs of its basic properties (invariance up to additive/multiplicative constants under change of underlying universal model, an analogue of the coding/counting/incompressibility theorem, and a characterization of algorithmically random infinite sequences in terms of $H^\infty$). The extension should be obtained by at least one of the following two routes, and the relationship between the resulting notions should be clarified:

(a) Non-terminating computation. Use universal devices that run forever and produce an infinite output stream; define the complexity of $\xi$ as the infimum length of a (possibly infinite) program description $p$ such that the never-halting computation of the universal device on input $p$ outputs $\xi$ in the limit.

(b) Infinite-time / real computation. Use a computational model that processes infinite inputs and produces infinite outputs in finite time, such as cellular automata acting on configurations in $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$, infinite-time Turing machines, or BSS-style computable functions on the reals; define $H^\infty(\xi)$ via the descriptive size of programs in such a model that output $\xi$.

Compare the two complexities, determine whether they coincide on natural classes of infinite sequences (computable, $\Delta^0_2$, Martin-Löf random, etc.), and decide whether either yields the "correct" notion in the sense that a $\xi$ is Martin-Löf random if and only if $H^\infty$ on initial segments — or on $\xi$ itself — exhibits an appropriate maximal-growth condition.
artifact.status_search_result: Standard algorithmic randomness theory provides notions of complexity for initial segments of infinite binary sequences (e.g., prefix-free complexity $K(\xi\!\restriction\! n)$, Schnorr/Martin-Löf characterizations), and infinite-time Turing machines together with BSS computation furnish frameworks (a) and (b) above. However, a single canonical "Chaitin complexity of an infinite string" unifying these viewpoints, with a full invariance theory and a randomness characterization satisfying the program described, does not appear to be definitively settled in the literature, so the status of the problem as posed is best regarded as unknown / partially addressed.

status_evidence.title: Kolmogorov complexity - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: An infinite sequence is random if the prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity of its initial segments grows quickly enough—there must be a constant c such that the complexity of an initial segment of length n is always at least n−c.
status_evidence.claim: Algorithmic randomness for infinite sequences is conventionally defined via the complexity of finite initial segments rather than via a complexity assigned directly to the infinite string.

status_evidence.title: Algorithmic information theory - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Algorithmic information theory studies Kolmogorov complexity and other complexity measures on strings (or other data structures).
status_evidence.claim: The standard objects of study remain finite-string complexities; extensions to genuinely infinite-string complexities via non-terminating or infinite-time models are not part of the standard canonical theory.
